prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It's true: I have it though I hardly approve of anything it does. Supposed bend of light or smudge where two odd angles cross. I hardly see— can hardly do a thing with it. White zone of no flesh pressing into no. So low, I can’t scale or measure it. I used to think: OK! A clean sharp place to keep. Or: I'll growa thing! to keep, for me! But no. It's just a ward to mark & mount, a loop I lope around with, so I count myself a realm of realms. I vote & vote. Turns out, we agree with everything we do, almost. We sweep the precincts of ourselves: the rooms between each rib & under them till we reach the fat red condo where our blood leans in. We live here now. Half heart, half townhouse. Come on down. Turn on that sweet TV. Our mise en place, our rugs & nooks: we’re full of stuff. We paint the furniture we couldn’t live without. It’s true at last: we have it all though we hardly know what any of it does.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker possesses something they neither understand nor approve of and can barely perceive or use.
- What once seemed like a clean space for growth instead becomes a boundary that defines and contains the self.
- The speaker portrays the self as a political realm whose inner parts repeatedly affirm their own actions.
- The body becomes a home, with ribs, blood, heart, rooms, furniture, and possessions blending into one domestic landscape.
- Despite feeling that they “have it all,” the speaker remains uncertain about the purpose of what they possess.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The speaker explores the elusive self and body through surreal images of borders, rooms, voting, and domestic space, trying to define and possess an identity that resists measurement or control. The poem concludes that we inhabit and endorse our crowded inner realms without fully understanding them, suggesting that selfhood is both abundant and fundamentally unknowable.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Supposed, White, But

outputs.L1: It’s true: I have it, though I hardly approve of anything it does. A supposed bend of light, or a smudge where two odd angles cross. I hardly see—can hardly do a thing with it. A white zone of no flesh pressing into no. So low, I can’t scale or measure it. I used to think: OK! A clean, sharp place to keep. Or: I’ll grow a thing! To keep, for me! But no. It’s just a ward to mark and mount, a loop I lope around with, so I count myself a realm of realms. I vote and vote. Turns out, we agree with almost everything we do. We sweep the precincts of ourselves: the rooms between each rib and beneath them, until we reach the fat red condo where our blood leans in. We live here now. Half heart, half townhouse. Come on down. Turn on that sweet TV. Our mise en place, our rugs and nooks: we’re full of stuff. We paint the furniture we couldn’t live without. It’s true at last: we have it all, though we hardly know what any of it does.
outputs.L2:
Yes, it belongs to me, though I scarcely endorse its actions: perhaps a curve in the light, perhaps a blur at the meeting point of two peculiar angles. Through it I barely perceive, barely manage anything. A pale vacancy, absent of flesh, pushing against nothingness. It lies so far beneath me that I can neither climb nor calculate it.

Once I told myself: Fine—a crisp, immaculate spot worth preserving. Or else: I’ll cultivate something here, something of my own to hold on to. Yet that never happened. Instead, it is merely a guarded boundary to label and display, a circuit I keep circling, allowing me to reckon myself one dominion among many dominions. Again and again, I cast my ballot. As it happens, we approve of nearly everything we undertake.

We patrol our inner districts, clearing the chambers between and beneath every rib until we arrive at the plump crimson apartment where the blood presses close. This is our home now: part heart, part row house. Step inside. Switch on that lovely television. Everything is arranged and ready—our carpets, corners, and alcoves—and we are crowded with possessions. We add color to the furnishings we believed essential to survival.

Finally, the claim is accurate: everything is ours, even though we have almost no understanding of what any of it is for.
outputs.L3:
The speaker possesses something they neither fully understand nor approve of—something so elusive that they can barely perceive it, let alone use it with confidence. What initially appears to be an open, clean space in which growth might occur gradually takes on a more restrictive meaning. Rather than offering freedom, this space becomes a boundary that defines the speaker’s identity while also containing and limiting it.

The self is then imagined as a political realm, divided into inner regions whose inhabitants continually justify and affirm their own behavior. This image suggests a consciousness made up of competing yet self-validating parts, each contributing to an unstable sense of authority and control. At the same time, the body is transformed into a home: ribs, blood, and heart merge with rooms, furniture, and possessions to form a single domestic landscape. The physical and psychological self thus becomes both the dwelling and everything held within it.

Although the speaker feels that they “have it all,” this apparent completeness brings neither clarity nor satisfaction. Possession does not lead to understanding, and abundance does not produce purpose. The speaker is left uncertain about what all these internal spaces, bodily structures, and accumulated belongings are ultimately for.
outputs.L4:
The speaker searches for a stable sense of self but repeatedly discovers that identity cannot be neatly located, measured, or possessed. Surreal images of borders, rooms, elections, and domestic interiors turn the body and mind into uncertain territories. Borders imply that the self should have clear limits, yet those limits continually shift or dissolve. Rooms suggest private spaces within the individual, but they are crowded, unfamiliar, and never entirely under the speaker’s control. Even the body, which might seem to offer the most concrete definition of identity, becomes strange and resistant to ownership.

The imagery of voting and endorsement adds a political dimension to this search. The speaker seems to ask who has the authority to decide what belongs within the self and which impulses, memories, or versions of identity are permitted to speak. Yet any attempt to establish order only reveals greater complexity. The inner world resembles a community whose inhabitants participate in its existence without fully knowing one another or understanding the system they sustain.

Domestic space further complicates the idea of possession. A home is usually associated with security, familiarity, and control, but here it becomes a metaphor for an interior life that remains partly inaccessible. The speaker may inhabit this space and call it their own, yet ownership does not produce complete knowledge. The self is therefore both intimate and alien: it is the place in which one lives, but also a place that can never be fully explored.

By the conclusion, the poem abandons the hope of arriving at a precise definition of identity. Instead, it accepts that the inner self is crowded, abundant, and mysterious. We live among our thoughts, desires, memories, bodily sensations, and competing identities, implicitly endorsing the whole complicated realm simply by continuing to inhabit it. Selfhood is presented not as a single object that can be mastered, but as an expansive and shifting territory—deeply ours, yet fundamentally unknowable.
outputs.L5:
It was supposed to be white—the dress, the flowers, even the sky in the photographs. Everything had been planned to look pure and perfect.

But rain fell before the ceremony, darkening the garden paths and staining the hem of the dress. Guests hurried beneath umbrellas while the wind scattered white petals across the wet ground.

For a moment, she thought the day was ruined. Then she saw him waiting, soaked and smiling.

It was not the day they had imagined, but it became the day they would always remember.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about the body as both a private home and a political territory, using anatomical imagery, wordplay, and an uneasy first-person voice.
counterfactuals.output:
My body is a house with the address redacted.

I sleep behind the sternum, in a narrow room where the heart keeps knocking as if it has forgotten the password. The ribs are white shutters. The lungs, two nervous curtains, open and close at every rumor of weather. Somewhere below, the liver stamps papers in purple ink. Somewhere lower, the border guards are arguing with the river.

I say *my* body, but the pronoun has been rezoned.

At night, officials pace the perimeter of my skin, measuring the acreage of a bruise. They call it public interest. They call it protection. They call it by names that do not answer when I call mine. Their laws enter through the keyhole and hang portraits in my uterus, my throat, my clenched left hand.

I have become a state of emergency.

My mouth is both embassy and checkpoint. Each tooth is a small white monument to what I was allowed to bite. The tongue, that soft dissident, keeps printing forbidden pamphlets: no, no, no—then swallowing them before dawn.

Inside me, the blood votes continuously, circulating its red ballots without secrecy. The veins are gerrymandered blue on the map, though opened they confess another color. Even my pulse has been polled. Even my hunger is subject to debate.

Still, I make a kitchen of the stomach. I set the table with salt and little moons of bread. I invite my ghosts to sit. We eat under the humming light of the spine, thirty-three locked doors pretending to be a ladder.

I am afraid to say I live here.

I am more afraid to say I don’t.

Sometimes I press my ear to my own wrist and hear the country beneath the country: workers of marrow striking matches, kidneys filtering the dark, ovaries keeping their bright, ungovernable calendars. The bones whisper, *occupy yourself*. The flesh replies, *I am already occupied*.

So I change the locks.

I name each scar a window. I teach the nerves to carry messages underground. I plant a flag in the navel—not victory, not surrender, only a scrap of cloth that says: someone is home.

Then morning conducts its census.

I stand before the mirror, that silver parliament, and raise my hand to swear I am the sole citizen of this trembling republic.

The reflection abstains.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental paragraph beginning with “It’s true: I have it,” in which the speaker struggles to understand the boundaries of the self.
counterfactuals.output: It’s true: I have it, though whether *it* is inside me or I am inside *it* depends on where the sentence puts its walls. I touch my wrist to locate the border, but the pulse knocks from both sides. Here is my name, I say, and the name turns like a key in someone else’s door. Here is my body—yet breath enters, hair leaves, light passes through the red rooms of the eyelids. Even memory refuses citizenship: my mother’s voice wears my mouth; a stranger’s grief sleeps under my tongue. If I draw a circle around myself, the hand remains outside it. If I widen the circle to include the hand, the pencil escapes. It’s true: I have it. Or it has me. Or “have” is only the little hinge trembling between two empty rooms.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, contemporary prose poem that blends the language of optics, voting precincts, real estate, interior decorating, and human anatomy. End by suggesting that we possess everything but understand almost nothing.
counterfactuals.output: At noon the city adjusts its aperture: precinct maps dilate across the glass towers, each district a lens ground to bend one kind of light toward one kind of ballot. We queue inside a converted showroom where the staging remains—bouclé chairs, quartz islands, a tasteful absence of evidence—and offer our signatures like capillaries feeding a paper heart. Outside, brokers speak of exposure, sightlines, good bones; upstairs, a couple measures the nursery while the mortgage tightens around their ribs. Every window manufactures a horizon. Every mirror returns a candidate. The poll workers peel names from the register; decorators peel years from the walls, uncovering beneath the greige a blue vein of plaster, beneath that brick, beneath brick the mineral dark. Our bodies, too, are subdivided: chambers, lobes, wards, parcels of nerve and rentable breath. We furnish the skull with flattering lamps. We hang conviction at eye level. Through the cornea’s wet constituency, the world campaigns in photons, promising depth, delivering surfaces. By evening the votes travel sealed through neighborhoods appraised by the square foot, while our pupils contract before screens that call their brightness clarity. We have the deed, the key, the floor plan, the full-length mirror; we have every organ named and every border numbered. We possess almost everything, and understand almost nothing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a strange lyrical monologue about having a nearly invisible scar or bodily boundary. Let it evolve into a meditation on ownership, identity, domestic life, and the many selves contained within one person.
counterfactuals.output:
There is a seam along my left wrist, pale as the memory of thread. You can only see it when I turn my hand beneath the kitchen light, where the bulb has begun to hum like an insect trapped in a glass.

No one else notices.

Once, someone asked whether it was a vein. I said yes. It seemed easier to let the body be accused of its own machinery. But it is not a vein. It is a border. On one side: the hand that opens the mail, salts the soup, tests the bathwater. On the other: the hand that belongs to no one, not even me.

I watch it at breakfast while the kettle invents weather. Steam climbs the window. The spoons lie in their drawer, nested and silver, each holding a small upside-down room. The house is full of such obedient objects. The cups consent to being cups. The chairs never wake appalled at their four legs. Even the knife, with its terrible clarity, does not wonder whether it is owned by the hand or whether the hand is merely the sheath from which it is drawn.

But I wonder.

I have signed my name on documents declaring that this body is mine. I have initialed the margins. I have carried it through airports and illness, through other people’s beds, through years that closed behind me like doors in a long hotel. Still, ownership feels too blunt a word. I own a blue bowl. I own three winter coats, though one of them has begun to smell like the basement. I own the dent in the hallway wall where the table struck it during our last argument.

But do I own the wrist?

Do I own the scar?

Perhaps the scar owns the moment that made it. Perhaps it keeps that hour folded inside itself, a small deed to the property. Perhaps beneath the skin there is a clerk in a dark office stamping each injury: RECEIVED, RECORDED, NEVER RETURNED.

At night I rub the seam with my thumb. It feels like nothing. That is its strangeness. A boundary with no fence, no river, no guard asleep in a wooden booth. Yet crossing it changes me.

Here is the self who washes dishes.

Here is the self who wants to break every plate.

Here is the self who remembers being nine years old and convinced the moon was following the car out of love.

Here is the self who has forgotten the faces of the dead for whole afternoons.

They live inside me badly, like relatives sharing a house after the will has been read. One keeps the curtains closed. One rearranges the furniture while I sleep. One eats standing over the sink. One is always packing a suitcase. One has never arrived.

Sometimes, while folding towels, I feel them pass through me. The child takes one end, the old woman takes the other, and between them we make a neat white square of time. Then I place it in the cupboard as if there will be enough clean linen for all of us.

Domestic life depends on this faith: that things can be put away. Flour in the jar. Shoes by the door. Grief in the body. The body in a name.

My name is written on the electricity bill, and every month the house fills with light that is supposedly mine. Yet light does not respect possession. It touches the scar without asking. It enters the refrigerator when I open it at midnight and finds me there, barefoot, drinking milk from the carton like an animal who has inherited a mortgage.

Who is standing there?

The good tenant? The thief? The woman I was? The woman who will someday leave this cup on the counter and never come back?

I turn my wrist. The seam appears, then vanishes.

Perhaps identity is only this: the angle at which the hidden becomes visible.

Perhaps I am not one country but a row of neighboring countries, all claiming the same river. There are checkpoints in my throat, disputed fields behind my eyes. Some mornings I wake under one flag, some mornings another. Their anthems are all made of my breathing.

Still, the kettle boils.

Still, someone must wipe the table.

I press my palm flat against the wood and feel the faint border brighten under the skin. For a moment, the house seems to press back. The walls, the pipes, the locked drawers, the dust with its patient citizenship—all of it holding me, all of it held.

I say: mine.

The room echoes: which one?
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a fragmented, darkly comic poem portraying the human body as a furnished townhouse and sovereign realm, with ribs as rooms, the heart as a condo, and consciousness as an electorate that keeps voting for itself.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Republic of Soft Furnishings**

The body is a narrow townhouse  
in a district zoned for grief.

Ribs: twelve rooms each side,  
bad plaster, no closets,  
wind paying rent in coughs.

The heart owns a condo downstairs—  
red walls, loud plumbing,  
a treadmill facing nowhere.

It complains to management.  
It is management.

Above, the lungs draw curtains  
and open them  
and draw them  
as if expecting weather to apologize.

The liver runs a night café  
for poisons and minor gods.  
The kidneys, twin clerks, stamp forms:

**ADMIT.**  
**EXPEL.**  
**TRY WATER.**

In the basement, the gut  
hosts a parliament of knives,  
all debating dinner.

Meanwhile—

the skull: a fortified capital,  
teeth at the gate,  
tongue delivering statements  
the government will later deny.

Consciousness constitutes the electorate.

Every morning it votes for itself.  
Unanimous.  
Turnout: one.

Every night it challenges the count,  
cites irregularities,  
demands a recount of childhood.

The feet are provinces.  
The hands, colonies  
with separatist ambitions.

The skin patrols the border  
in a cheap beige uniform,  
letting in sunlight,  
keeping out almost nothing.

Still, the realm issues decrees:

**Stand.**  
**Swallow.**  
**Smile for the photograph.**

The sovereign sits nowhere,  
wearing a crown of static,  
signing laws in disappearing ink.

In the heart-condo  
the pipes knock three times.

Someone upstairs laughs.

Someone downstairs says  
that is not laughter.

The townhouse leans  
into its mortgage of earth,

fully furnished,  
briefly occupied,

and listed—  
with charming original damage—  
at an impossible price.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
